\subsection{Mechanical momentum or learned signal? Nagel and matched twins}

\citet{nagel2025seemingly} shows that when $P\gg T$, a ridgeless RFF forecast
is a similarity-weighted average of the training-window returns. Persistent
predictors make similarity track recency; time variation in predictor
volatility scales the position. We implement his benchmark rather than only a
declining-return proxy: its position multiplies the linearly declining twelve
month return average by $0.05$ divided by the mean within-window variance of
the fifteen predictors. We also follow Nagel in leaving the dependent return
unstandardized and in averaging completed statistics across RFF draws.

Panel A of Table~\ref{tab:nagel-experiments} contains the three direct tests.
On historical returns the RFF strategy has information ratio
\NagelRawHistIR, which falls to \NagelRawHistSpanIR{} after controlling for the
market and Nagel payoff. The fixed artificial return path adds the MA(2)
reversal $\xi_t-0.2\xi_{t-1}-0.2\xi_{t-2}$ with innovation variance
$0.01$; its RFF information ratio is \NagelRawMAIR.
The wild-bootstrap experiment fits each predictor to a bias-adjusted AR(1)
and independently sign-flips its fitted innovations for every RFF draw. It
therefore removes broad classes of predictive content while preserving each
innovation's magnitude and volatility path. Its RFF information ratio is
\NagelRawWildIR, and the market-plus-Nagel spanning alpha has
$t=\NagelRawWildSpanAlphaT$. These are \NagelExperimentSeeds{}-draw Monte
Carlo estimates; the draw count is configurable up to the paper's larger run.

Slides 17--18 ask a sharper identification question that is separate from
Nagel's paper. We construct matched markets
\[
 r^{(+)}_{t+1}=a g(X_t)+\epsilon_{t+1},\qquad
 r^{(-)}_{t+1}=-a g(X_t)+\epsilon_{t+1},
\]
with the same predictor and shock histories. The planted $g$ is fixed before
estimation: a bounded curved dividend-price term plus a bond--credit
interaction. Subtracting paired forecasts cancels the fitted common shock
when both markets use the same fourteen inputs, so
$(\hat f^{(+)}-\hat f^{(-)})/2$ directly tests recovery of $a g(X_t)$. A
robustness design adds each world's own lagged return as input fifteen, making
the predictor panels different. Panels B--C report pattern, scale, error, and
the market-plus-Nagel payoff alpha separately in both twins. For example, the
realistic-signal fourteen-input recovery has correlation
\NagelTwinRealCleanCorr, slope \NagelTwinRealCleanSlope, and normalized RMSE
\NagelTwinRealCleanNRMSE; its plus/minus spanning alpha $t$-statistics are
\NagelTwinRealCleanPlusAlphaT{} and \NagelTwinRealCleanMinusAlphaT.
The normalized clean-design recovery statistics are identical across signal
strengths by construction: with one shared design, ridgeless forecasts are
linear in the target, the common fitted shock cancels, and the amplitude
scales both recovered and planted signals equally. The fifteen-input design
breaks that exact cancellation because its feature maps differ by world.

\paragraph{Interpretation and verdict.} Taken together, the empirical tests
favor Nagel's mechanical explanation of the historical payoff. The raw-return
RFF information ratio falls from \NagelRawHistIR{} to
\NagelRawHistSpanIR{} after controlling for the market and Nagel payoff, and
the residual alpha is not statistically distinguishable from zero
($t=\NagelRawHistSpanAlphaT$). Adding the MA(2) reversal drives the RFF
information ratio to \NagelRawMAIR, while replacing the predictor innovations
with wild-bootstrap sign flips leaves performance surprisingly close to the
historical result (\NagelRawWildIR{} versus \NagelRawHistIR). Thus the
historical strategy payoff is largely consistent with recency, predictor
persistence, and predictor-volatility timing; it is not, by itself, strong
evidence that the estimator learned an economic predictor--return mapping.

The matched twins nevertheless reject the stronger claim that the estimator
is incapable of learning nonlinear signal. In the favorable easy-signal design
with fourteen identical inputs, recovery has correlation
\NagelTwinEasyCleanCorr, slope \NagelTwinEasyCleanSlope, and normalized RMSE
\NagelTwinEasyCleanNRMSE; both worlds retain positive market-plus-Nagel alpha
($t=\NagelTwinEasyCleanPlusAlphaT{}$ and
$\NagelTwinEasyCleanMinusAlphaT{}$). This support for KMZ is qualified rather
than general. The recovered signal is substantially attenuated, adding each
world's own lagged return reduces correlation to \NagelTwinEasyLagCorr{} and
slope to \NagelTwinEasyLagSlope, and positive residual alpha no longer appears
in both worlds ($t=\NagelTwinEasyLagPlusAlphaT{}$ and
$\NagelTwinEasyLagMinusAlphaT{}$). At realistic signal strength even the clean
design has alpha $t$-statistics of \NagelTwinRealCleanPlusAlphaT{} and
\NagelTwinRealCleanMinusAlphaT. Our overall reading is therefore asymmetric:
Nagel better explains the observed historical payoff, while KMZ receives a
narrower existence result---the high-complexity estimator can recover a strong
nonlinear rule in a clean controlled environment, but the evidence for an
economically distinct payoff is fragile to signal strength and the
lagged-return input.
